hookLine: riots sweep Spain; people are killed and others forced to convert
carry: remembered, by name and by place

cards: City by city, a father lists what has happened. He is writing to Jews in another country: Hasdai Crescas, a philosopher and a community leader in Aragon, with a duty to report.

He names it all: the mobs, the burned streets, the people killed, the people dragged to the font and baptized under threat. Partway through, he writes about Barcelona, and about his own son, killed there.
The letter is careful, almost formal, and then it is not. Today's lesson has a year for its name: thirteen ninety-one.

teach.b: It started in Seville. For some time a church official there, Ferrand Martínez, had been preaching against the Jews of the city, against the wishes, records say, of some above him.
When the moment came, crowds broke into the Jewish quarter. From there the violence ran along the roads, through Castile and into Aragon, town after town, through the summer.
Some local rulers tried to protect Jewish quarters; others could not or did not.

Crescas's letter is one of the witnesses, and it names two kinds of loss: the dead, and the living who were forced, at the edge of a sword, to accept baptism. That second loss is the one this day asks us to hold.
In Hebrew the forced ones are called anusim. Those who converted, under threat or under years of pressure, became known in Spain as conversos, New Christians.

Some held on to Jewish customs in secret, lighting a candle on Friday behind closed shutters. Some became sincere Christians. Other families were somewhere in between, and were looked at with suspicion by both sides.

Jewish law starts from a principle the Rambam's code sets down: a person forced is not judged like a person who chooses. Later rabbis argued hard over those who stayed Christian when they might have left.
And the communities that survived kept going, rebuilding synagogues and teaching their children, though Spain would never again be what it had been. This is not a story to turn into a slogan.
It is a story to be remembered, carefully, by name and by place.

how: Jews remember the persecutions of Spain in study and in memorial gatherings, and some descendants of conversos today explore and recover their family's Jewish history.

practice: Hold in mind someone who was made to give up who they were, in that summer in Spain or anywhere since: a name you know, or one you never will.

Picture one small thing they might have kept, a candle behind a shutter, a recipe passed down without its reason, and stay with them. If you pray, you can remember them in your own words; if you don't, simply hold them.

wordCard.voice: Anusim. The forced ones, Jews baptized under threat during the riots that swept Spain in 1391, remembered alongside those who were killed. Today's word.
